### Level: `r my_level`

### Justification

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

get_json_info <- function(df){
  #make empty list
  results <- list() 

  #iterate through the df to get each state, lat, long, and plug each into url.
  for(i in 1:nrow(df)){
    state <- df$state[i]
    latitude <- df$latitudes[i]
    longitude <- df$longitudes[i]
    url <- paste0("https://api.g7vrd.co.uk/v1/satellite-passes/25544/", latitude, "/", longitude, ".json")
    
    # make an API request for each url
    response <- GET(url)
    
    #if the response works
    if (http_status(response)$category == "Success") {
      
      # grab the json content, the first 3 satellite passes
      json_data <- fromJSON(rawToChar(response$content))
      passes_data <- head(json_data$passes$tca,3)
      
      # Store the relevant data in the list
      results[[i]] <- list(state = state, latitude = latitude, longitude = longitude, passes = passes_data)
    }
    
    #if the response didn't work
    else {
      cat("Error fetching data for latitude:", latitude, ", longitude:", longitude)
      
      results[[i]] <- list(state = state, latitude = latitude, longitude = longitude, error = http_status(response)$message)
    }
  }
  #after the looping, return the list
  return(results)
}

api_data <- get_json_info(state_capitals_clean)

# used Gemini to help with the above function
```

This function shows an example of when my partner and I used apis from the satellite website to scrape data on passtimes. This gave us good practice at using api functions like `fromJSON()` and `http_status()` to scrape for API data. It took some practice at first to understand just what the url was scraping and how we needed to scrape over multiple times. Originally we were scraping passtimes for just one city at a time. This was not the goal of the lab so we had to iterate over the whole dataframe (or all capitals) in the function using our API scrape functions.

# Code Design, Algorithms, Iteration (CDAI):

*These objectives ask you to design code-based approaches to statistical computing problems, usually involving iteration to a stopping condition.*

## \[CDAI-1\] R Programming Language

-   I understand non-standard evaluation (aka "tidy eval" or "unquoted objects"), and I can use tunneling in my functions.
-   I understand functional programming, and I can use functions as objects in my code design.

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: CDAI-1

my_level <- 2

portfolio_levels <- portfolio_levels %>%
  bind_rows(
    tibble(Objective = "CDAI-1", 
           Level = my_level)
    )
```

### Level: `r my_level`

### Justification:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

library(dplyr)
library(rlang)

remove_outliers <- function(data, ..., sd_thresh = 3){
  vars <- enquos(...)
  
  filtered_data <- data
  
  for (var in vars) {
    var_name <- quo_name(var)
    
    if (!is.numeric(pull(filtered_data, !!var))) {
      warning(glue::glue("Variable '{var_name}' is not numeric."))
      next
    }
    
    var_mean <- mean(pull(filtered_data, !!var), na.rm = TRUE)
    var_sd <- sd(pull(filtered_data, !!var), na.rm = TRUE)
    
    filtered_data <- filtered_data %>%
      filter(abs((!!var - var_mean) / var_sd) < sd_thresh)
  }
  
  return(filtered_data)
}
```

This function uses the `...` and `enquos()` to ensure that other specified parameters will be used later down in the function. This allows the user to specify as little or as many variables in the dataset and remove outliers for those variables. 

## \[CDAI-2\] Object Handling

-   I have built in checks for possible input problems
-   I can make reasonable choices in my code design about when to save intermediate objects.
-   I can convert objects between types and structures as needed.

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: CDAI-2

my_level <- 3

portfolio_levels <- portfolio_levels %>%
  bind_rows(
    tibble(Objective = "CDAI-2", 
           Level = my_level)
    )
```

### Level: `r my_level`

### Justification:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

library(dplyr)
library(rlang)

remove_outliers <- function(data, ..., sd_thresh = 3){
  vars <- enquos(...)
  
  filtered_data <- data
  
  for (var in vars) {
    var_name <- quo_name(var)
    
    if (!is.numeric(pull(filtered_data, !!var))) {
      warning(glue::glue("Variable '{var_name}' is not numeric."))
      next
    }
    
    var_mean <- mean(pull(filtered_data, !!var), na.rm = TRUE)
    var_sd <- sd(pull(filtered_data, !!var), na.rm = TRUE)
    
    filtered_data <- filtered_data %>%
      filter(abs((!!var - var_mean) / var_sd) < sd_thresh)
  }
  
  return(filtered_data)
}
```

I wanted to use the same function since this function also shows how to meaningfully save intermediate objects and check for input object types. Like before we use the `...` and `enquos` for tunneling within our function. This comes with some problems as we have to check for input types since users are now able to input any type of variable they choose. To check for this we put a warning to check only for numeric variables based on the variable names the user input. To properly check for variables being numeric we also have to properly save the variables properly inside the function. This is done at the beginning of the function by using the `vars <- enquos(...)`, so now we can properly check the variable type or use other functions on the inputs by using `vars` later in the function.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Define the base URL
base_url <- "https://www.cheese.com/alphabetical/"

# Function to scrape a single page
scrape_page <- function(page_number) {
  page_url <- paste0(base_url, "?page=", page_number)
  Sys.sleep(1)
  
  # Read the HTML content from the webpage
  webpage <- read_html(page_url)
  
  # Pull cheese names 
  cheese_names <- webpage %>%
    html_elements("h3 a") %>%
    html_text()
  
  # Pull cheese URLs
  cheese_data <- webpage %>%
    html_elements("h3 a") %>%
    html_attr("href") %>%
    paste0("https://cheese.com", .)
  
  # Pull cheese images
  cheese_images <- webpage %>%
    html_elements("#main-body img") %>%
    html_attr("class")
  
  # Return the dataframe with names, URls, and images
  return(data.frame(
    Name = cheese_names,
    URL = cheese_data,
    Image = cheese_images,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Apply the scrape_page function to all pages of cheese.com
all_cheese_data <- lapply(1:103, scrape_page)
```

This combination of functions shows another example of when we had to iterate over a function in our lab assignment. The function written scrapes one singular page of the cheese.com website. Unfortunately the task was to scrape for all 103 pages of the website and there was not an fairly easy solution for me at first to move through the pages within the function. My idea was then to iterate the scraping of one page for all 103 pages. This was done using the `lapply()` function over the numbers of all numbered pages since the function uses the page number to scrape the desired page. The `lapply()` function uses a vector of all the page numbers and then the function `scrape_page()` that was made for iteration.

### Justification:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

hourglass_x <- function(angle) {
  # Formula I played with until it looked right.
  x <- sin(angle) * abs(cos(angle))^1.2
  return(x)
}

# Function to calculate the y-coordinate for an hourglass shape.
hourglass_y <- function(angle) {
  y <- cos(angle)
  return(y)
}

# Creates a tibble representing the base hourglass shape.
hourglass_shape <- tibble(
  angle = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 50),
  x = hourglass_x(angle),
  y = hourglass_y(angle)
)

# Generates data for a single "Perlin noise" hourglass.
perlin_hourglass2 <- function(n = 100,
                              freq_init = 0.3,
                              octaves = 2,
                              r_min = 0.5,
                              r_max = 1,
                              w_min = 0,
                              w_max = 4,
                              rot = 0,
                              x_shift = 0,
                              y_shift = 0,
                              id = NA,
                              seed = NULL) {

  if(!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  tibble(
    angle = seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = n),
    
    radius = fracture(
      x = cos(angle),
      y = sin(angle),
      freq_init = freq_init,
      noise = gen_perlin,
      fractal = fbm,
      octaves = octaves
    ) |>
      normalize_radius(r_min, r_max),

    # Calculates final x and y coordinates based on radius, hourglass shape, and shifts.
    x = radius * hourglass_x(angle) + x_shift,
    y = radius * hourglass_y(angle) + y_shift,

    width = fracture(
      x = cos(angle + rot),
      y = sin(angle + rot),
      freq_init = freq_init,
      noise = gen_perlin,
      fractal = fbm,
      octaves = octaves
    ) |>
      normalize(to = c(w_min, w_max)),

    id = id
  )
}
```

So this function shows the main changes I made to apply multiple functions creating the generative art. I created an animated hourglass shape based on a specified palette of colors. The palette of colors corresponds to the number of hourglasses created and the color of each hourglass. The two shape functions at the beginning make the shape of the hourglass and the `perlin_hourglass2()` function creates the single hourglass. There is another function I have that connects all three of these that accepts a palette as one of the input as well as the number of hourglasses to create. All of these functions when combined create a beautiful colored and animated hourglass shape with random noise.
